questions.question: A learner has time for only a few short runs to improve a fine-tuned model. Which plan uses that time best?
options: Try learning rates of 0.001, 0.002, 0.003 and 0.004, because small linear steps are more precise.
Tune dropout, weight decay, batch size and model depth together in one large grid.
Tune the number of epochs first, then the learning rate if time remains.
Try learning rates on a log scale, such as 1e-4, 3e-4, 1e-3 and 3e-3, on a data subset, then confirm the best with extra seeds.
questions.explanation: The learning rate usually matters most, and a log scale covers the useful range in few runs. The most tempting wrong option is the linear set of values: it looks careful, but all four rates are in a narrow band, so it could miss a much better rate that is 10 times smaller or larger.

questions.question: Which set of habits best allows another person to repeat a training run exactly and reuse its model?
options: Fix seeds, keep all settings in a config dictionary, log each run to a results table, and save the best checkpoint together with its config outside the session.
Save the final notebook output as a screenshot and keep the model in the Colab session.
Record only the best validation score, because failed runs are not useful.
Save a checkpoint after every epoch to the local Colab disk.
questions.explanation: Seeds, a single config, a results table and a checkpoint stored with its config make a run describable, comparable and reloadable. The most tempting wrong option is saving every epoch's checkpoint: the local Colab disk is deleted when the session ends, and a checkpoint without its config does not say which settings or preprocessing it needs.

questions.question: Before training any deep model for the capstone, which step is most important to do first?
options: Fine-tune the largest pretrained model available to get a high score quickly.
Upload the dataset to the Hugging Face Hub so it is backed up.
Check the dataset's licence, source and personal-data risks, then build a simple baseline and write an experiment plan.
Evaluate several candidate models on the test set to choose a direction.
questions.explanation: A usable dataset, a baseline score and a plan with hypotheses make every later result meaningful. The most tempting wrong option is starting with the largest model: without a baseline, you cannot show it is worth its cost, and without checking the licence first, you may have to restart with different data.

questions.question: Two fine-tuned models have validation macro F1 scores of 0.842 ± 0.006 and 0.845 ± 0.007 over 3 seeds. The second uses a more complex schedule. Which choice is best justified?
options: Choose the second model, because its mean score is higher.
Choose the simpler first model, because the scores are within seed variation, and state this reason in the report.
Evaluate both on the test set and choose the one with the higher test score.
Choose neither and report the baseline, because the difference is small.
questions.explanation: When results are within seed variation, the simpler model is a reasonable choice, and the reasoning should be written down. The most tempting wrong option is testing both and picking the higher test score, which turns the test set into a validation set and makes the reported test result too optimistic.

questions.question: Which addition would most improve a capstone report that already contains the final test score and a confusion matrix?
options: A longer description of how neural networks work in general.
Only the best run, with failed runs removed to keep the report short.
The Hugging Face access token used during the project, so others can reproduce the upload.
An experiments table with every run, known limitations and out-of-scope uses, and instructions to run the notebook from the start.
questions.explanation: A model-card-style report needs the full experiment history, the limits and a reproducible path, not just the final numbers. The most tempting wrong option is removing failed runs to keep it short: failed runs are evidence for how the final model was chosen, and hiding them makes the report less credible.
